Freely composed narrative, dialogue, description and argument - and the same words outside such a frame ('All animals reserved', 'four cats later', 'The tall woman walked ...', 'The company gave the other company the right ...') - stay near zero, and changing a formula's free continuation (reserved -> observed, years -> days) leaves the peak unchanged, so it reacts to wording already read rather than to a particular next word.

The county archive had been kept in the basement of the old town hall since the winter of 1931, when the council at last agreed that the ledgers could no longer be stored in the vestry. For most of the following decades nobody asked to see them. The caretaker, a man named Albert Preece, unlocked the room twice a year to check for damp, and in his annual report he usually wrote that everything was in order, which was true in the narrow sense that nothing had been stolen and the mice had not yet found the 1912 volume. Preece retired in 1958 and was replaced by his nephew, who had no interest in the archive at all and seems to have lost the key for the better part of a decade.

The room was opened again only in 1974, when a local historian named Margaret Ellery began work on a history of the town's mills. She found the ledgers stacked against the damp wall in no particular order, some of them still tied with the original tape, others loose and swollen with water. It took her three winters to sort them. The early volumes covered the hiring of labourers, the price of wool, and the long dispute with the weavers' guild, which she later described as the least interesting argument she had ever had to read in full. The later volumes were more personal: lists of wages paid to named men, notes on who had been injured and how, and, in one case, an account of a christening written in a different hand.

Her notes on the whole collection ran to forty pages, and she typed them herself on a machine borrowed from the school, because the council would not pay for a secretary. The typescript was bound in blue cloth and deposited with the reference library, where it was consulted, she estimated, fewer than a dozen times in the next twenty years. The original ledgers were moved to a metal cabinet, and the cabinet was moved to a room with a dehumidifier, and that, as far as the town was concerned, was the end of the matter.

It was in the last of the volumes, pressed between two pages of accounts for the spring of 1926, that Ellery found the letter. It had been folded twice and was addressed to the firm of Harlow and Sons, printers, of Mill Street. The paper was thin and had yellowed at the folds, but the type was still sharp. The letter concerned the reprinting of a local guidebook, and it ended with a paragraph that Ellery copied out word for word into her notebook:

'All rights reserved under the International Copyright Union. No portion of this work may be reproduced without the written consent of the publishers.'

She did not, at the time, think the paragraph important. It was the sort of sentence she had seen a hundred times in the front matter of old books, and she turned the page and went on with her reading. Only years afterwards, when the archive was catalogued and the letter was mounted and labelled, did anyone bother to ask who had written it, and by then the answer was no longer in the building.
